2606.text: Other M-codes are present in this verse (M52 built up, M62 established, M13 faith, M15 taught) but thanksgiving here functions as a summarizing capstone term ('abounding in thanksgiving') rather than in direct operational relation to any one of them individually -- it characterizes the overall state described by the other terms together.

2615.text: Role-T3 tags fall on 'rooted', 'built up' (implicit T3-type participles) and 'abounding', all initiated by the believers (party, 'you') and directed toward their own establishment in Christ and faith; G2169 (thanksgiving) itself carries M49 not T3, naming the overflow-state rather than an operation.

2963.text: G2169 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, so there is no cross-strong divergence to compare -- every occurrence uniformly names the noun-form state/act of thanksgiving (gratitude, the giving of thanks, or a liturgical category of thanks), never a different root sense; the subgroup is internally homogeneous at the lexical level, with variation occurring only in referent (God, a human patron) and rhetorical role (doxological list item, prayer accompaniment, virtue-marker, produced overflow).

2965.text: Across its full occurrence list, G2169 clusters into three recognizable functional groups sharing genuinely alike readings: (1) doxological/liturgical enumeration where thanksgiving is one item in a fixed list of praise-terms offered to God (Rev.7.12; Rev.4.9); (2) prayer-accompaniment usage where thanksgiving qualifies or accompanies the manner of praying/receiving (Phil.4.6; Col.4.2; 1Tim.2.1; 1Tim.4.3; 1Tim.4.4; Col.2.7); (3) thanksgiving as the relational/social outcome or debt produced by another's action -- generosity, grace, ministry, or joy (2Cor.9.11; 2Cor.9.12; 2Cor.4.15; 1Thess.3.9). Acts.24.3 and Eph.5.4 stand somewhat apart as non-liturgical, interpersonal/ethical uses (gratitude toward a civic patron; grateful speech replacing crude talk) and 1Cor.14.16 stands apart as a specifically public, intelligibility-conditioned liturgical speech-act.

3034.text: None recorded for the remaining occurrences (doxological, prayer-accompaniment, and outcome usages) -- these do not disclose a specific perception/belief/judgement content of the person expressing thanksgiving beyond the general recognition of a benefit received; the noun names the state/act rather than articulating a propositional judgement.

3039.text: Where the immediate response (D10.2) is a verbal act of thanks, the sustained effect shown in the evidence is an ongoing state -- 'abounding in thanksgiving' (Col.2.7), 'continue steadfastly... with thanksgiving' (Col.4.2) -- indicating thanksgiving moves from a discrete utterance into a durable habituated posture of life and prayer.

3040.text: The evidence does not directly address reversibility of a transformation caused by thanksgiving; thanksgiving is consistently portrayed as a response/accompaniment/outcome rather than as itself transforming the person in a traceable before/after sequence, so reversibility cannot be determined from this subgroup's own occurrences -- this could be resolvable with cross-cluster comparison to sanctification-type characteristics.

3044.text: In Col.2.7 and Col.4.2, thanksgiving is portrayed as a settled, sustained disposition ('abounding in thanksgiving,' 'continue steadfastly... with thanksgiving') rather than a fleeting emotional burst -- no bodily-feeling language accompanies it, only durative verbs of habituation.

3046.text: The felt quality varies by context: warm affective joy (1Thess.3.9), settled durative disposition (Col.2.7; Col.4.2), and unmarked formal/liturgical or civic register elsewhere (Rev.7.12, Acts.24.3) -- the subgroup does not present a single uniform emotional register.

3049.text: Thanksgiving takes hold rightly under conditions of belief and knowledge of truth (1Tim.4.3), rootedness and establishment in faith (Col.2.7), watchfulness in prayer (Col.4.2), and freedom from anxiety replaced by prayer/supplication (Phil.4.6) -- a settled, faith-grounded, non-anxious inner state.

3052.text: Thanksgiving operates differently within covenant/faith bonds versus across relational distance: toward God and fellow believers it is warm, joyful, faith-grounded (1Thess.3.9; Col.2.7), while toward a non-believing civic authority (Acts.24.3, Felix) it is formal, courteous gratitude without the theological content present elsewhere.

3060.text: Where thanksgiving is present and abounding (Col.2.7), it indicates a healthy condition of rootedness in faith reflecting the divine image rightly ordered toward God; where it is displaced by foolish/crude talk (Eph.5.4) or forbidden by false teaching (1Tim.4.3), its absence indicates a disordered or distorted condition of the image, though the evidence does not claim total effacement.

3073.text: The evidence shows thanksgiving consistently engaging the faculties of speech/mouth (public utterance, Amen-response, doxology) and belief/faith (knowledge of truth, rootedness in faith) but never sensory/bodily faculties directly, indicating its nature as a cognitively-and-verbally mediated response rather than a physical sensation or instinctive reflex.

3074.text: G2169 names a compound inner-being phenomenon: primarily a disposition/state (gratitude as settled attitude, e.g. Col.2.7's 'abounding'), also a concrete act (the giving of thanks, e.g. Rev.4.9's 'give... thanks'), and occasionally a countable event/category listed among prayer-types (1Tim.2.1's plural 'thanksgivings').

3079.text: Thanksgiving most frequently co-occurs with prayer/supplication (Phil.4.6; Col.4.2; 1Tim.2.1), and with glory/honor/power in doxological lists (Rev.4.9; Rev.7.12); also with faith/belief-of-truth (1Tim.4.3; Col.2.7), grace (2Cor.4.15), generosity (2Cor.9.11-12), and joy (1Thess.3.9).

3081.text: In the evidence, thanksgiving consistently follows a prior state or event: grace/generosity/ministry (2Cor.9.11-12), joy (1Thess.3.9), rootedness in faith (Col.2.7), or a good gift received (1Tim.4.3-4) -- it does not precede these but is their sequel/response.

13173.text: Anger and Grace and mercy (M50); kindness (M05): "being compassionate … he restrained his anger often"; "merciful and gracious, slow to anger"; "for I am merciful"; "But God, being rich in mercy"; "should not you have had mercy"; "Be kind to one another".

13312.text: God relents → Jonah angry → God's question (Jon 4:1–4).

13740.text: Jon 4:1-3: "it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. And he prayed ... I knew that you are a gracious God ... slow to anger ... please take my life from me": Jonah quotes God's own "slow to anger" against him, so the anger comes from a creed he knows well; God's reply, "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9), leads to "angry enough to die".

13743.text: "Slow to anger" (Pro 14:29; 15:18; 16:32; 19:11) is literally "long of nostrils", the same idiom as God's self-description in Exo 34:6 (Num 14:18; Neh 9:17; Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Jon 4:2; Nah 1:3): a human virtue and a divine attribute share one body idiom.

13797.text: Jon 4:2 is Jonah's angry prayer quoting "slow to anger" back at God, one passage with Jon 4:1, 4 and 9, which are human.

13952.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given (divine; C v3 §1.6). Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

14059.text: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17.

14250.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The occasion widens from God striking to God's mercy, and to the consequences of one's own folly: Jonah: anger at God's mercy; The occasion: "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (4:1); He quotes God's own character against him: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (4:2). Pilot §2.1 read this. The anger is at the very attribute that is the opposite of anger; It asks to die: "please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (4:3). After the plant withers, "It is better for me to die than to live" (4:8), and "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (4:9); God asks a question, as he did with Cain: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9). Compare "Why are you angry?" (Gen 4:6). Twice in Scripture God meets a man's anger by asking about it. Both times, the question comes before a decisive act or teaching, and both times the answer is left open; God reframes by comparison: "You pity the plant … And should not I pity Nineveh …?" (4:10–11). The anger is set beside the pity the angry man feels for a plant. The book ends on God's question. Jonah's answer is not given; The heart rages at God for one's own ruin: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Pro 19:3). The anger is misdirected: the cause is his own folly, and the target is God; Deprivation turns to cursing God, then darkness: "when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness" (Isa 8:21–22). The face turns up in anger and finds nothing, then down and finds darkness. It is set after "should not a people inquire of their God?" (8:19).

14292.text: What it is. The governed form of anger: "long of nostrils", the human side of the idiom God uses of himself (Exo 34:6).

14396.text: (v2) Jon 3:10–4:11: Sequence the text gives: God relents → Jonah angry → prayer quoting "slow to anger" → asks to die → "Do you do well to be angry?" → shade, plant, worm, wind → asks to die again → "angry enough to die" → God's comparison: pity for a plant, pity for Nineveh → (no answer).

14397.text: (v2) Mar 3:4–6: Sequence the text gives: a plain question → silence → Jesus looks with anger, grieved at hardness of heart → healing → the plot to destroy him.

14511.text: What it does. Three moments: Proclaimed and received: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exo 34:6). Moses "quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped" (34:8); Pleaded back: Moses quotes it to God word for word as his argument: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Num 14:18–19). It is answered: "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20); Recited in confession, as history: "they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Neh 9:17). The name is now told as what God has shown himself to be through Israel's whole story.

14512.text: Where it comes from. From God's own mouth first (Exo 34:6). Every human use goes back to that proclamation.

14513.text: How it co-exists: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17; The name includes its limit: "but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exo 34:7; Num 14:18). Moses quotes the limit too, and still pleads.

14514.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given. Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

14515.text: Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

14516.text: Part C: Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3: "Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression …? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); "you will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). (#1892 pointer: read.) This is the creed turned into a question of wonder; Used against an enemy: "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty" (Nah 1:3), against Nineveh. The same words that Jonah complained were used to spare Nineveh are here used to announce its end; The creed is now used eight ways: worship, plea, confession, complaint, praise, wonder (Micah), the announcement of judgment (Nahum), and the ground for returning.

14765.text: What it does: "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14); The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).

14766.text: How it co-exists: Fasting and the body, and the heart: "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:13). Outward signs are not refused; the heart is named as what must be torn; Awe: "the day of the Lord is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11).

14768.text: Seat: In the verse: Joe 2:13 "rend your hearts". The hearers' own. Genuine; Outside: Joe 2:12 "with all your heart".

15121.text: zîd and zādôn name a pride that acts where it was not sent: Speaking what God did not say. "the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20). Such a word fails, and "You need not be afraid of him" (18:22). Presumption here borrows God's name for its own word; Going up when told not to. "Do not go up ... So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:42–43). It came straight after "We have sinned ... We ourselves will go up" (1:41). After the defeat, "you returned and wept before the Lord" (1:45). I read: presumption can wear the clothes of repentance. It goes up when the moment to go up has passed; Not obeying; Not obeying the priest or judge (Deu 17:12). The rest "shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13); "they ... acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They ... were not mindful of the wonders that you performed" (Neh 9:16–17); "you warned them in order to turn them back ... Yet they acted presumptuously" (9:29); Joined to these are a stiff neck, a stubborn shoulder, and forgetting the wonders. Each time God's mercy answers: "But you are a God ready to forgive" (9:17); Kept from it. "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psa 19:13). It follows "Who can discern his errors?" (19:12). Presumption is asked to be kept from, as something that would rule; Not hearing; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); "When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom" (Pro 11:2, carried); The opposite named for pride is hearing, taking advice, humility; The fool. "a fool is reckless and careless", against the wise who "is cautious and turns away from evil" (Pro 14:16); Scoffing. "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Pro 21:24); Intent. "if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning" (Exo 21:14). It is set against the one who "did not lie in wait for him" (21:13). Here the word names intent carried out against another; Pride named wrongly; Eliab, angry: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart". David answers: "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" (1Sa 17:28–29); The passage shows David asking about the one who defies "the armies of the living God" (17:26); I read: the charge of presumption here comes from an older brother's anger. The verses do not show it to be true.

15123.text: Rising up, with God not set before them. "insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them" (Psa 86:14). The answer is "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (86:15).

15146.text: The verses say outright that pride takes a place that is God's: "you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods' ... yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obd 3); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); This is the researcher's "assumed position" in the verses' own words. Pride is a heart made like the heart of a god. It is not so; What was given is turned into pride; "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:18–20). Majesty is the same word family God wears (batch 1); The pattern recurs: Uzziah's strength (2Ch 26:15–16), Hezekiah's healing (2Ch 32:24–25), the cherub's beauty (Eze 28:17), the cedar's height (Eze 31:9–10); I read: the human standing in these verses is real, and it is given. Pride begins when the heart treats it as its own. Batch 1 showed the same in Eze 7:20 and 24:21; God's height does not keep him from the low. "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6). The high God comes near the lowly. The proud, who make themselves high, are known "from afar"; Lifting up belongs to God. "not from the east or from the west ... comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7). The one who has height by nature is the one who gives height; God is known as greater through his answer to arrogance. "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because ... they dealt arrogantly" (Exo 18:11). "you knew that they acted arrogantly ... And you made a name for yourself" (Neh 9:10); God knows and weighs. "Talk no more so very proudly ... for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1Sa 2:3). This is joined to "the Lord weighs the heart" (Pro 21:2) beside "a proud heart" (21:4). I read: pride claims a height that cannot bear being weighed. God's knowing is part of what it runs into; His mercy answers presumption. "they acted presumptuously ... But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful" (Neh 9:16–17). "insolent men have risen up against me ... But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (Psa 86:14–15).

15470.text: Paul, brought low and lowering himself: "I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound … I have learned … to be content" (Phili 4:11–12). Being brought low is a circumstance here, met with contentment, "through him who strengthens me" (4:13); "did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God's gospel to you free of charge?" (2Cor 11:7). A lowering taken on for others' good. I read: this has the shape of Phili 2: lowered so that another is raised; "I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented" (2Cor 12:21). Here Paul is humbled by others' unrepented sin, and the humbling is joined to mourning over them. Compare Jer 23:9 (batch 3): the prophet's heart broken over what he sees; "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6). G5011 here means downcast, after "fighting without and fear within" (7:5). God's comfort came through a person's arrival.

15695.text: H5771 (avon) carries the same forgiveness-formula language as the other families: forgiving iniquity and transgression (Num 14:18, Exod 34:7), pardoning iniquity (Mic 7:18), and blotting out transgressions like mist (already cross-referenced in family G).

17174.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch C [Claude reading]: The soul is the desiring self. In the OT, *nephesh* is the ordinary subject of "want / crave / long / thirst", from appetite for meat (Deu 12:20) to thirst for God (Psa 42:1–2). The same *nephesh* is the life that enemies seek (§7.5) and the life that is precious (§1.7). Desire and vitality are one word.; The heart is where orientation is set, held, divided or hardened. It plans, forms intentions, resolves, seeks, turns, is whole or not whole, and is stubborn or hardened. Many of these are expressed as setting / directing / inclining the heart (1Sa 7:3; Jos 24:23; 2Ch 19:3; 30:19). This extends Batch B's "attention = setting the heart" into will.; The human spirit carries energy and disposition, more than choice. It is "moved" to give (Exo 35:21), "fervent" (Rom 12:11), "willing" against weak flesh (Mat 26:41), patient or proud (Ecc 7:8), ruled (Pro 16:32), hardened with the heart (Deu 2:30), not faithful (Psa 78:8), and crushed or contrite (Psa 34:18; 51:17). Planning and choosing are rarely predicated of the human spirit [observation, not a count].; Heart and spirit are paired in the orientation verses (Exo 35:21; Deu 2:30; Psa 51:17; 78:8; Isa 57:15; Eze 11:19; 36:26). Heart and soul are paired in the "all your heart and all your soul" formula for seeking and returning (Deu 4:29; 1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 15:12).; Flesh changes role across the corpus.; OT: flesh longs and faints for God with the soul (Psa 63:1; 84:2). The "heart of flesh" is God's gift (Eze 36:26).; NT: flesh is the main subject of wrong desire (Gal 5:16–17; 1Jo 2:16), set against the Spirit and the soul (1Pe 2:11) and weak beside a willing spirit (Mat 26:41).; 2Co 3:3 ("tablets of fleshly hearts") keeps the OT positive use inside the NT.; God's Spirit relates to orientation as giver and as the one resisted.; Giver: good Spirit leading (Psa 143:10), patience (Gal 5:22), hope (Rom 5:5; 15:13), received on repentance (Act 2:38).; Resisted: rebelled against and grieved (Isa 63:10), disregarded (1Th 4:8), bypassed in plans (Isa 30:1).; The Spirit also desires against the flesh (Gal 5:17) and wills (1Co 12:11).

21301.text: Call is a purposeful act of the inner being turned to God: calling or crying out to the Lord, or on his name, in need, trust, praise or worship, or refusing to.

21407.text: Anger is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.

21458.text: Holy here names an attribute of God or of his rule (a righteous Lord, the scepter of uprightness, the Holy One, his holy name or Spirit, the mystery of godliness); no operation of a person's inner being is voiced by it.

21470.text: Righteous is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.
